html:
In 1837 James Prinsep, an official of the Calcutta mint, worked out how to read Brahmi, the oldest script of India after the Indus signs. With it he recovered the emperor Ashoka, who had been forgotten for more than a thousand years.

Pillars and rocks across India carried writing that no living scholar could read. Brahmi is the ancestor of nearly every script of South and Southeast Asia, but its early form had gone out of use.

Prinsep was secretary of the Asiatic Society and had copies of inscriptions sent to him from all over the country. He noticed that dozens of short texts on the stone railings at Sanchi ended in the same two letters. He guessed they recorded gifts and that the word was danam, "gift". That gave him two letters, then others, and within weeks the whole alphabet.

He then read the long texts on the pillars (see the Edicts of Ashoka). They were the orders of a king called "Beloved of the Gods, Piyadasi". A British official in Ceylon found the same name used for Ashoka in a Buddhist chronicle.

Indian history now had a fixed point in the 3rd century BCE. Prinsep wore himself out with the work and died in 1840, aged forty.
